title: Teen’s DIY AI Detects 1.5 Million Flickering Sky Objects in NASA Archive, Astronomers Take Notice
body:
A high‑school student in Pasadena has turned a modest home‑grown artificial‑intelligence program into a powerful tool for scanning NASA’s vast trove of sky images, flagging more than 1.5 million transient light sources that could represent previously unknown astronomical phenomena. The discovery, made by 17‑year‑old Matteo Paz while participating in the Planet Finder Academy, has captured the attention of professional astronomers who are now sifting through the flagged candidates for anything that might expand our understanding of the dynamic universe.

Paz’s AI, built on an open‑source machine‑learning framework, was trained to detect brief “flickers” – sudden spikes in brightness that last only a few seconds to minutes – within the massive data set collected by NASA’s Wide‑field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Over the course of several weeks, the program combed through more than 500 terabytes of archival imagery, isolating 1.5 million events that met its criteria. While most of these are likely to be known sources such as variable stars, satellite glints, or instrumental noise, a small fraction could point to rare or entirely new classes of objects, ranging from fast‑moving near‑Earth asteroids to exotic stellar explosions.

The breakthrough emerged from the Planet Finder Academy, a summer initiative hosted by the California Institute of Technology that pairs gifted high‑school students with seasoned researchers to tackle real‑world problems in astrophysics. Under the guidance of Caltech astronomer Davy Kirk, Paz refined his algorithm by feeding it a curated training set of confirmed transients and false positives. “The key was teaching the AI to distinguish genuine astrophysical signals from the sea of artifacts that inevitably appear in space‑based imaging,” Kirk explained. “Matteo’s ingenuity lay in designing a lightweight model that could run on a standard laptop yet still process data at a scale normally reserved for supercomputers.”

The scientific community’s reaction has been cautiously optimistic. Dr. Elena Marconi, a senior researcher at the Space Telescope Science Institute, noted that the sheer volume of flagged events offers a “gold mine” for follow‑up studies. “Even if only a handful turn out to be truly novel, the payoff is immense,” she said. “Historically, serendipitous discoveries – like the first pulsars or the unexpected brightness dips of Tabby’s Star – have reshaped entire fields. An AI that can systematically surface such anomalies could accelerate that process dramatically.”

Nevertheless, experts warn that the path from detection to confirmation is fraught with challenges. Many of the 1.5 million candidates will require cross‑verification with other telescopes, spectral analysis, and sometimes even new observations to rule out mundane explanations. The sheer workload could overwhelm existing pipelines, prompting calls for collaborative platforms where citizen scientists and professional astronomers can share the burden. Initiatives such as Zooniverse have already demonstrated the power of crowd‑sourced classification, and integrating Paz’s AI output into such frameworks could streamline the vetting process.

Looking ahead, the success of Paz’s project may inspire a new wave of student‑led AI research in astronomy. Educational programs are already exploring ways to embed machine‑learning curricula into STEM outreach, recognizing that the next generation of sky‑watchers will need both domain knowledge and data‑science skills. Moreover, NASA is reportedly evaluating the incorporation of similar AI tools into its upcoming missions, such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to enhance real‑time transient detection.

If even a fraction of the flagged flickers prove to be genuine, Matteo Paz’s modest code could help chart previously hidden corners of the cosmos, underscoring how youthful curiosity, when paired with cutting‑edge technology, can ripple outward to the broader scientific enterprise. As astronomers begin to sift through the mountain of alerts, the universe may soon reveal surprises that were waiting, unnoticed, in the archives for decades.
